analysis.one_liner: Replaces the mortgage interest deduction with a 20% credit and redirects savings to affordable rental housing.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the last two weeks of the 112th Congress, the bill was referred to two committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end the mortgage interest deduction — a tax break that mostly benefits high earners — and replace it with a flat 20% tax credit on mortgage interest, capped at interest on $500,000 of debt. The deduction would shrink each year from 2013 to 2017, and the cap on deductible mortgage debt would drop from $1 million to $600,000. The money saved would be redirected to affordable housing: 60% to the Housing Trust Fund, 30% to Section 8 rental assistance, and 10% to repairs for public housing, with an increase in the low-income housing tax credit.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and extremely low-income families, who face a shortage of affordable homes and long waiting lists for assistance. Middle- and lower-income homeowners also gain, because a flat 20% credit reaches far more of them than an itemized deduction that only pays off for households with large mortgages and high tax bills.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters, extremely low-income families, and moderate-income homeowners

how_it_helps.text: Converts the mortgage interest deduction into a 20% nonrefundable tax credit on up to $500,000 of mortgage debt, so moderate-income homeowners who take the standard deduction today can receive a benefit for the first time [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings state that more than 75% of the value of the current mortgage interest deduction goes to the top 20% of earners, and fewer than half of taxpayers with a mortgage claim it at all [S3].
Savings from the change would be split: 60% to the Housing Trust Fund, 30% to Section 8 rental assistance, and 10% to the Public Housing Capital Fund for repairs [S2] [S3].

The bill cites a shortage of nearly 7 million homes affordable to families in the bottom 20% of income — only 30 affordable units for every 100 families — plus $26 billion in deferred maintenance at public housing agencies, losing roughly 10,000 units a year [S3].

It would raise the low-income housing tax credit ceiling from $1.75 to $2.70 per capita and boost the credit by 50% for buildings serving extremely low-income households, and allow co-op residents to deduct interest and taxes on the land their building sits on [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Higher-income homeowners with large mortgages, especially in expensive housing markets, who would see their deduction shrink yearly to zero by 2018; the real estate, mortgage lending, and homebuilding industries that profit from a subsidy tied to expensive home purchases would also face reduced demand at the top of the market.

drawbacks.text: The five-year phaseout would raise taxes each year on homeowners who currently itemize, including some middle-class owners in high-cost states, at a time (2012) when the housing market was still recovering from the crash [S3].
The new credit is nonrefundable, so it only helps households that owe income tax — the lowest-income homeowners still get nothing from it [S3].
A rapid reduction of the deductible-mortgage cap from $1 million to $600,000 could depress home values in high-price markets, a cost to existing owners the bill does not address [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is real: an estimated $70-billion-a-year tax expenditure skewed toward the top fifth of earners would be redirected to housing aid for people at the bottom, while most homeowners with typical mortgages would come out roughly even or better under the credit. The main honest objection is transition risk — phasing down the deduction during a still-fragile housing recovery could have hurt home values — but the bill's five-year gradual phaseout was designed to blunt that.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 18, 2012, sixteen days before the Congress ended, referred to the Ways and Means and Financial Services Committees, and neither committee ever took it up, so it died when the 112th Congress expired on January 3, 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill on December 18, 2012, with Rep. Robert Scott as the sole cosponsor [S1] [S4] [S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Financial Services Committee, and the record shows no hearing, markup, or floor action in either [S5].
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, and the bill was not reintroduced in that session, so it expired without a vote [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy homeowners who capture most of the mortgage interest deduction kept it intact, and the real estate and mortgage industries kept the demand the deduction supports. The estimated billions in annual tax savings the bill would have redirected to low-income housing aid never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-income homeowners and the housing finance industry

for.name: Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to convert the mortgage interest deduction into a credit and fund affordable housing programs.

for.name: Robert C. Scott
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the only additional supporter it attracted.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Dave Camp, R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 18, 2012, and took no further action — no hearing or markup — before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral for the housing-related provisions and took no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both supporters were Democrats — Ellison and Scott — and no Republican cosponsored; no vote ever occurred, so the partisan split is inferred from sponsorship, not a roll call.

industries.note: The bill's own findings state they receive more than 75% of the mortgage interest deduction's value; the phaseout would redirect that tax benefit to low-income housing aid. Their gain under the status quo comes at the direct expense of renters and public housing.

industries.industry: Real estate agents, mortgage lenders, and homebuilders
industries.note: The deduction subsidizes demand for large, expensive mortgages and home purchases at the top of the market; replacing it with a capped credit would shrink that demand. These industries have historically been among the deduction's most active defenders, though no lobbying appears in this bill's record.

industries.industry: Affordable housing developers and low-income housing tax credit investors
industries.note: A higher per-capita credit ceiling and a 50% credit boost for extremely low-income units, plus dedicated Housing Trust Fund and public housing repair money, would expand their business — and the housing it produces.

industries.industry: Cooperative housing corporations and their resident-owners
industries.note: Residents could deduct interest and taxes on the land under their co-op building, ending an exclusion that treated co-op owners worse than conventional homeowners.
